facts.statement: The genus Phyllolepis was described by Louis Agassiz in 1844.
facts.quote: authority: Agassiz 1844

facts.statement: Phyllolepis is the type genus of the extinct arthrodire placoderm family Phyllolepida, which lived during the middle to late Devonian periods.
facts.quote: Phyllolepis (from the Greek roots for 'leaf' and 'scale') is the type genus of Phyllolepida, an extinct taxon of arthrodire placoderm fish from the middle to late Devonian.

facts.statement: Species of Phyllolepis lived approximately 360 million years ago during the Famennian stage of the Late Devonian.
facts.quote: The species of Phyllolepis, themselves, are restricted to the Famennian-aged freshwater strata of the Late Devonian, around 360 million years ago.

facts.statement: Fossils of Phyllolepis have been found primarily in Europe and North America.
facts.quote: Fossils of this genus have been found primarily in Europe and North America.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis went extinct at the end of the Devonian period during a mass extinction event.
facts.quote: The end of the Devonian saw them disappear in a mass extinction.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis lived in freshwater environments such as rivers and streams.
facts.quote: Phyllolepis lived in freshwater environments, possibly rivers and streams.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis were presumed to be blind, bottom-dwelling predators that detected prey using sensory organs located in the grooves of their armor plates, which created a distinctive wooden surface appearance.
facts.quote: As with all other known phyllolepids, Phyllolepis were presumed to have been blind, bottom-dwelling predators that detected prey through sensory organs in the surface grooves of their armor plates (which gave their plates a distinctive "wooden surface" appearance).

facts.statement: Phyllolepis typically grew to be 30 to 40 centimeters in length and had a very flat body shape.
facts.quote: Phyllolepis, as was typical of Phyllolepida, tended to be 30 to 40 cm in length and very flat.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis possessed extensive armor composed of full, flat plates instead of scales, along with a wide jaw and mouth.
facts.quote: Phyllolepis have extensive armor made of full, flat plates, rather than scales, with both a wide jaw and mouth.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis featured long, narrow anterior dorsolateral plates and dermal ornamentation consisting of smooth, concentric rings on their plates.
facts.quote: They also feature long, narrow anterior dorsolateral plates and a dermal ornamentation of smooth, concentric rings upon their plates.

facts.statement: The presence of elongated basiptergia on related phyllolepid placoderms suggests that Phyllolepis may have possessed them as well.
facts.quote: Elongated basiptergia have been found on some phyllolepid placoderms, such as Austrophyllolepis and Cowralepis, suggesting Phyllolepis may have had them as well.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis had eyes located on either side of their heads and lacked a scleral ring, unlike modern flounders.
facts.quote: As with other members of Phyllolepida, Phyllolepis have eyes on either side of their heads, unlike modern flounders, as well as an absent scleral ring.

facts.statement: The highly developed system of lateral ridges on Phyllolepis is suggested to have been used for electroreception to sense their surroundings in the absence of functional eyes.
facts.quote: The highly developed system of lateral ridges are suggested to have been used for electroreception, in order to sense their surroundings in absence of functional eyes.

facts.statement: It is difficult to identify phyllolepid placoderms like Phyllolepis unless a full fossil assemblage is known, as many defining traits must be used in conjunction with others.
facts.quote: However, because many defining traits for Phyllolepis must be used in conjunction with other traits (for example, the genera Phyllolepis, Placolepis, and Cobandrahlepis all lack a posterior median ventral plate), it is difficult to identify phyllolepid placoderms unless a full fossil assemblage is known.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis were likely ambush predators that lay in wait in the substrate as bottom-dwellers.
facts.quote: These fishes were likely ambush predators, lying in wait in the substrate as bottom-dwellers.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis used their long tails for rapid propulsion to catch prey.
facts.quote: Their long tails would be used for rapid propulsion to catch their prey.

facts.statement: Dig sites in Europe and the Pennsylvania Catskill formation may have hosted coastal-marine species of Phyllolepis, based on siltstone and sediment composition.
facts.quote: However, dig sites in Europe- and even locations still in the Pennsylvania Catskill formation- may have been home to coastal-marine Phyllolepis species, based on the composition of siltstones and sediment deposits.

facts.statement: It is possible that Phyllolepis could live in both freshwater and marine environments, or that intercontinental land connections allowed their movement.
facts.quote: It is possible there were land connections intercontinentally, or the fishes were euryhaline or marine-tolerant.

facts.statement: Northern Hemisphere phyllolepids are found in Famennian rocks, while Australian and Antarctic samples date from the late middle Devonian through the late Famennian.
facts.quote: All of the phyllolepids found in the Northern Hemisphere have been found in rock dated to the later Devonian Period (Famennian), however Australian and Antarctic samples date earlier, from the late middle Devonian up through the late Famennian.

facts.statement: The oldest confirmed phyllolepid fossil dates to the middle Devonian period.
facts.quote: The oldest confirmed Phyllolepid is from the middle Devonian.

facts.statement: The genus Phyllolepis has only been found in strata dated to the Famennian age so far.
facts.quote: The genus Phyllolepis has so far only been found in Famennian age strata.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis concentrica is characterized by concentrically arranged ridges on its plates and occasional patches of tubercles.
facts.quote: The first Phyllolepis to be found. This species has concentrically arranged ridges parallel to the postero-lateral plate margin, with occasional patches of tubercles.

facts.statement: The nuchal plate of Phyllolepis concentrica has a straight to slightly convex anterior margin and is only slightly broader at the front than the back.
facts.quote: The nuchal plate has a straight to slightly-convex anterior margin, and is only slightly broader anteriorly than posteriorly.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis undulata features widely spaced ridges and a nuchal plate that is taller than it is broad.
facts.quote: Widely spaced ornamentation in the forms of ridges, as well as a taller than broad nuchal.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis orvini, named in 1934, possesses ridges on the anterior nuchal plate and central and lateral protrusions on its anterior margin.
facts.quote: Named by Sensiö in 1934, this species has ridges on the anterior portion of the nuchal plate, as well as one central two lateral protrusions on the anterior margin of the nuchal.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis neilseni has proportionately broader anterior ventrolateral plates, an elongated outline, a convexly curved anterior margin, and a concavely curved posterolateral margin.
facts.quote: Proportionately broader anterior ventro-lateral plates than P. Rossimontina. Elongated plate outline, convexly curved anterior plate margin, and concavely curved posterolateral plate margin.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis rossimontina features a meshwork reticulated pattern on its dorsal plates and linear-style ornamentation on its ventral plates.
facts.quote: The dermal ornamentation of the dorsal plates is composed of a meshwork reticulated pattern and linear-style ornamentation on the ventral plates.

facts.statement: All phyllolepid species, except P. orvini, have preorbital plates that meet medially.
facts.quote: The preorbital plates are found to meet meially (minus P. orvini, all phyllolepid species share this trait).

facts.statement: Phyllolepis was the first genus recognized in the order Phyllolepidae until 1984.
facts.quote: Phyllolepis was the first genus to be recognized in the order Phyllolepidae until 1984.

facts.statement: Louis Agassiz discovered the first species of Phyllolepis, P. concentrica, in 1844 at Clashbennie, Scotland.
facts.quote: Phyllolepis concentrica was the first species discovered of the genus, by Louis Agassiz in 1844 at Clashbennie, Scotland.

facts.statement: Many complete, articulated phyllolepid specimens were found in the middle Devonian at the Mt. Howitt site in Australia during the 1970s.
facts.quote: In the 1970s many complete, articulated Phyllolepid specimens were found from the middle Devonian at the Mt. Howitt site in Australia.

facts.statement: Material from Mt. Howitt was defined as the genus Austrophyllolepis, which helped solidify the group's classification within Placodermi and the Arthrodira clade.
facts.quote: This material was gradually defined as genus Austrophyllolepis, based on plate proportions, but also solidified the assignment of the group to Placodermi and as a clade inside Arthrodira.

facts.statement: Sensiö demonstrated in the 1930s that phyllolepids possessed jaws and belonged to the group Placodermi.
facts.quote: Sensiö continued, with several publications in the 1930s, to show that phyllolepids had jaws, and belonged with placoderms.

facts.statement: Phyllolepis is classified in the class Placodermi.
facts.quote: classis: Placodermi†

facts.statement: Phyllolepis belongs to the order Arthrodira.
facts.quote: ordo: Arthrodira†

facts.statement: Phyllolepis is a member of the family Phyllolepididae.
facts.quote: familia: Phyllolepididae†

facts.statement: Phyllolepis lived in freshwater environments, possibly in rivers and streams.
facts.quote: Phyllolepis vivió en ambientes de agua dulce, posiblemente en ríos y arroyos.

facts.statement: Like other phyllolepid species, Phyllolepis is considered a blind bottom-dwelling predator that detected prey using sensory organs located in the grooves of its armor plates, giving them a distinctive wood or leaf-like surface appearance.
facts.quote: Al igual que con todos los demás filolépidos, las especies de Phyllolepis se consideran como depredadores ciegos, que vivían en el fondo del agua y que detectaban a sus presas a través de órganos sensoriales presentes en los surcos de la superficie de sus placas de blindaje (que dan a sus placas un aspecto distintivo de "superficie de madera u hojas").

facts.statement: Phyllolepis lived from the Givetian to the Famennian stages, between 387.95 and 358.86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Givetian to Famennian (387.95 to 358.86 million years ago)

facts.statement: In 2005, P. delicatula was declared a nomen nudum because it lacked defining features.
facts.quote: In 2005, this species became nomen nudum due to a lack of defining features.

facts.statement: P. konincki has recently been suggested to be a synonym of P. undulata.
facts.quote: Recently suggested to be a synonym for P. undulata.

facts.statement: P. rossimontina is currently under contention, with some researchers suggesting it should be synonymized with P. undulata based on overlapping broadness characteristics.
facts.quote: This species is currently under contention: it has been called to be included as a synonym of P. undulata by Olive et al. (2015), due to its characteristic broadness being within acceptable range of P. Undulata specimens found.

facts.statement: The scarcity of complete Phyllolepis specimens and the visibility of key features only on specific plates has led some paleontologists to call for the redesignation of currently named species.
facts.quote: The low number of complete Phyllolepis specimens found combined with key identifying features only visible on specific plates has made it difficult to confidently identify species, causing some paleontologists to call for redesignations of the current named species of Phyllolepis.
